# Known Trade-Offs

> Accepted limitations documented during the Hone critique/defender loop for **provenant**.
> Each entry records what the limitation is, why it was accepted, what mitigates it, and what would trigger revisiting.

<!-- Entries are added by the Defender during the loop. Do not edit retroactively. -->

## Trade-off: Audit-pack tamper-evidence relies on internal hash chain only (no external notary)

**Limitation:** The v0 audit pack's tamper-evidence is a SHA-256 hash chain over canonicalized JSON, persisted in the customer's own Postgres and object store. There is no RFC 3161 trusted timestamping, no third-party notarization, no external witness, and no cryptographic signature from a Provenant-controlled or regulator-controlled key. An attacker with root and database write access on the customer's host can reconstruct a fully self-consistent chain from scratch; tampering by a privileged host operator leaves no external witness. This means "tamper-evident" in v0 is internally tamper-evident, not externally attested.
**Why accepted:** v0 targets single-tenant and air-gapped deployments operated by the customer themselves. In that threat model, the customer is the operator and the auditor of last resort; the customer's separation-of-duties controls (separate audit team, replicated audit log, periodic chain verification) are what give the chain its evidentiary weight. Adding an external notary (RFC 3161 TSA, a hosted Provenant attestation service, blockchain anchoring) before validating customer demand and regulator expectations would expand the surface area without confirmed need. The thesis claim is "tamper-detectable by the customer's audit team," which the hash chain satisfies; the stronger claim "tamper-evident to an external regulator without internal cooperation" is not made in v0.
**Mitigation:** (a) The threat-model section ([`architecture/cross-cutting/security.md`](architecture/cross-cutting/security.md)) explicitly scopes out root-equivalent compromise and documents the chain as detection-not-prevention. (b) Operational guidance includes audit-log replication to a separate write-once store and a separate-team audit-verification cadence. (c) The audit pack format is designed to accept additional attestation artifacts (signed PDFs, TSA tokens) as drop-in additions without schema change.
**Would revisit if:** A regulator or customer compliance team formally rejects an audit pack because it lacks an external notary; or competitive products ship RFC 3161 / TSA integration as table stakes; or Provenant moves into a multi-tenant SaaS model where Provenant itself is the operator and customers need an external witness against Provenant.
**First raised:** cycle 1

## Trade-off: Streaming and split-turn parallel tool_use deferred (v0 is single-turn, non-streaming parallel only)

**Limitation:** v0 supports parallel tool dispatch only when every member of a parallel sibling group is emitted as a fully-formed `tool_use` block within a single model response turn. Two model behaviors are out of scope: (a) streaming tool_use, where a tool_use block is emitted progressively before being fully formed at dispatch time; (b) split-turn parallel, where a model emits parallel tool_use blocks across multiple response turns under load. The kernel treats each turn's tool_use blocks as an independent `sibling_group_id` (no cross-turn merging) and forces streaming off at the model-abstraction layer on compliance-path runs.
**Why accepted:** The parallel-sibling deterministic-order rule in [`architecture/subsystems/audit.md`](architecture/subsystems/audit.md#parallel-sibling-deterministic-order) requires `sibling_group_id` to be a pure function of one response envelope's canonicalized bytes. A cross-turn merging rule would either make `sibling_group_id` depend on a non-local future-turn observation (breaking byte-identity on replay where the second turn might arrive at a different point in the canonicalized history) or require post-hoc rewriting of an already-hashed audit entry (forbidden by the append-only chain). Streaming tool_use additionally breaks the intra-sibling ordering invariant (`tool_call_started` precedes `token_mint` entries which precede `tool_call_completed`) because at dispatch time the tool_use block does not yet exist as a complete object. Designing a deterministic merging rule that survives turn-splitting AND a streaming-tool_use ordering rule is real architectural work; v0 prioritizes shipping single-turn non-streaming parallel correctly over partial coverage of the split-turn case.
**Mitigation:** (a) The harness forces `stream=false` at the `ModelClient` layer on compliance paths regardless of the underlying client's capability advertisement. (b) When a model does emit parallel batches across turns (which Claude variants occasionally do under load), the runs still complete deterministically: each turn forms its own sibling group with its own `sibling_group_id`, and replay produces byte-identical chains. The trade-off is that the agent loses Claude's ability to maximally parallelize across the natural turn boundary, not correctness. (c) The harness documents the constraint and emits a typed `harness.streaming_disabled` log event on every run start so operators can confirm the configuration.
**Would revisit if:** Mode B hosts ship streaming tool_use by default and v0.5 needs to support them without a deployment-shape exception; or measurement shows that split-turn parallel is common enough that treating each turn as an independent group materially degrades agent latency for real recon traffic; or a deterministic cross-turn merging rule is designed and validated against the byte-identity property.
**First raised:** cycle 3

## Trade-off: Live progress observability for buffered parallel blocks

**Limitation:** Parallel-sibling `tool_call_started` / `tool_call_completed` / `tool_call_failed` / `token_mint` entries are buffered in kernel memory for the duration of a parallel batch and flushed to `audit_entries` only after every sibling completes (the buffer-and-flush rule in [`architecture/subsystems/audit.md`](architecture/subsystems/audit.md#parallel-sibling-deterministic-order)). Operators tailing `audit_entries` cannot see per-sibling progress inside an in-flight batch; a stuck tool call inside a parallel block is invisible from `audit_entries` alone until the batch completes or `max_wall_clock` fires. Worst case: up to `max_wall_clock` (default 300s) of silence between the last pre-batch entry and the flush.
**Why accepted:** Streaming the buffered entries to a live audit-channel during the batch would either reintroduce wall-clock-completion-order non-determinism into `seq` (defeating the whole reason buffering exists) or require a separate, non-replay-deterministic side channel — both of which are real work that exceeds v0 scope. The deterministic chain is the load-bearing artifact for regulators; live operator observability is a separate concern that does not require chain entries.
**Mitigation:** (a) The kernel exposes the in-memory buffer's per-sibling status (sibling_index_in_group, started_at_wall, in_flight | completed | failed) as a Prometheus gauge `provenant_parallel_sibling_state{run_id,sibling_group_id,sibling_index}` updated in real wall-clock time. Operators alert on long-in-flight siblings via this gauge, not via `audit_entries`. The gauge is explicitly labeled "not part of the replay-deterministic chain; emitted live; not buffered." (b) `max_wall_clock` bounds the silence window. (c) The Phase-4 done-when requires that the gauge surface at least the sibling count and per-sibling started/completed/failed transitions during a parallel block.
**Would revisit if:** Operators report that the Prometheus gauge is insufficient diagnosis surface for production incidents; or a future regulator requires that the live audit channel itself reflect in-flight tool execution; or v0.5 introduces a deterministic merging rule that makes streaming the buffered entries viable.
**First raised:** cycle 3

## Trade-off: Host conformance attestation is self-declared in v0 (no operator-signed JWT, no Provenant-side verification)

**Limitation:** The `host_conformance_attestation` field on `EntryKindRunStarted.deterministic` ([`architecture/subsystems/audit.md`](architecture/subsystems/audit.md#host_conformance_attestation)) records what the host operator declares about which version of `provenant mcp-conformance` they have most recently passed. The kernel does not verify the claim cryptographically and does not run the suite itself against the host. A non-conforming Mode B host that lies on its `host_conformance.yaml` produces audit packs that claim attestation without having earned it. A genuinely untested host produces `exit_kind: host_text_only` runs that still complete; the only audit-pack-visible signal is `host_conformance_attestation.mode = mode_b_untested`.
**Why accepted:** Cryptographically-strong host attestation requires either (a) an operator-controlled signing key whose issuance and rotation is its own subsystem, or (b) a hosted Provenant attestation service that customers' hosts call to record conformance — both expand scope materially without a confirmed customer or regulator demanding them in v0. The self-declared field captures the regulator-relevant fact ("which conformance suite did the host operator claim to have passed at the time of this run?") in a way that is at least tamper-evident on the chain. For deployments where unsigned host-channel output is unacceptable, Mode A is already the documented required shape ([`thesis.md`](thesis.md)).
**Mitigation:** (a) `provenant audit pack` prominently displays the attestation mode on the pack README and PDF cover sheet so a reviewer cannot miss `mode_b_untested`. (b) Mode A runs the kernel fills the attestation in itself; Mode A is the recommended shape for regulator-facing work. (c) The mcp-conformance suite is publicly reproducible; an external auditor can independently verify a host's claim by re-running the suite against the same host build.
**Would revisit if:** A regulator or customer compliance team rejects an audit pack because `host_conformance_attestation` is self-declared; or competitive products ship a signed conformance attestation by default; or a hosted Provenant attestation service is launched as part of the v0.5 commercial offering.
**First raised:** cycle 3
